# Taggbox Developer API v3 — LLM-ready specification

Paste this whole file into an AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot)
together with your task, e.g.:

  "Using the API described below, build a social WIDGET I can drop
   into any page of my site, in Node.js/Express (or PHP), showing the
   latest 30 Instagram image posts. My access token is in the
   ACCESS_TOKEN environment variable."

  ...or say "build a social widget PAGE / a full-width section on my site"
  instead — rule 1 below covers both, and they differ only in what gets
  rendered, never in where the token lives.

Everything an integration needs is in this file; no other docs are required.
Agents: fetch this file RAW (curl the URL you were given); a summarising fetch
drops the field names, which are the one thing that cannot be guessed.
Human-readable docs: https://github.com/wallapi/taggbox.com-API-Docs

## Facts

- Base URL: https://api.taggbox.com/api — a fixed value, the same for every
  account. It is NOT shown in the dashboard and there is nothing to copy:
  put it in the API_BASE_URL environment variable so a different host can be
  pointed at for staging, and default to the production one above.
- Protocol: HTTPS, JSON only. All endpoints are GET. The API is READ-ONLY —
  there are no create/update/delete endpoints.
- Auth: every request needs a credential, one of:
  (a) the account's user key, i.e. its account-wide access token — reaches
      every widget on the account;
  (b) a wall token (starts with "wt1_") — taken from the dashboard: open
      the gallery's card, click its three-dots menu, choose "Access Token".
      That menu item exists only on plans that include API access. Same
      auth, but every query is pinned to that one widget automatically; there
      is no widget parameter to pass and no way to widen the scope.
  Preferred: header  Authorization: Bearer <CREDENTIAL>
  Also accepted: query  ?access_token=<CREDENTIAL>
  Both are server-side secrets. NEVER put them in browser JavaScript. The
  standard shape is a page rendered on your own server: it holds the token,
  calls this API, caches the result and sends finished HTML. The browser
  never talks to this API, and never needs to.
- Rate: 1–2 requests/second is fine. Plans have a daily hit ceiling; when
  exhausted the API answers 401 with an explanatory message.
- Every success response is wrapped in an envelope; the payload is in `body`:
  { "status": true, "message": "Operation successful", "code": 200, "body": { ... } }
- Errors: 401 — the message says which of these it is: "Missing credentials
  — send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`" (no credential sent), "Invalid
  Token" (a wall token that is tampered, revoked, or whose gallery is gone),
  "API access is not allowed" (bad account key, or API disabled on the plan),
  "API access limit exceeded" / "Plan limit exceeded" (daily ceiling used up
  — the quota is counted from midnight UTC, so that is when it frees up);
  404 (post not on this account), 422 (invalid parameters). A 422 body lists
  EVERY bad parameter:
  { "status": false, "code": 422, "message": "Validation Failed",
    "body": { "fields": [ { "field": "limit", "code": "isInt", "detail": "..." } ] } }
- Ids are prefixed strings in responses (post_4421, wall_123, feed_88,
  network_2). Request parameters accept prefixed or bare numeric ids.
- Responses always contain the FULL post object. There is no `fields`
  parameter.

## Endpoints

### GET /v3/posts — list approved posts

Optional query parameters (all filters AND together):
- feed_ids     csv of feed ids. A feed is one network's source on the gallery,
               so THIS is also how you filter by network: pass the feed ids
               of the network you want. Every post carries both feed_id and
               network, so the mapping is discoverable from the posts.
               There is no `networks` parameter and no `wall_id` parameter.
- media_types  csv of: text, image, video.
- sort         csv, `-` prefix = descending. Sortable: created_at,
               modified_at, id, pinned. Default: -pinned,-created_at
               (pinned first, then newest).
- limit        page size, default 50, silently capped by the plan.
- after        opaque cursor from the previous response's paging.next_cursor.
               Bound to the sort that minted it; changing sort mid-pagination
               => 422. Never construct a cursor yourself.
- pinned_only  1 = only pinned posts.
- min_rating   integer 0–5, reviews only.
- created_after / created_before   ISO 8601 or unix seconds.
- expand       csv of: products (UGC shopping tags), album (merge carousel
               sibling media into the post's `media`). Each costs extra
               queries; off by default.

Response body: { "posts": [Post, ...], "paging": { "limit": n,
"has_more": bool, "next_cursor": string|null } }

Pagination algorithm: request page; while body.paging.has_more, repeat the SAME
request adding after=body.paging.next_cursor.

### GET /v3/posts/:postid — one post

:postid = post_4421 or 4421. No query parameters — the list route's
parameters (`expand` included) are ignored here, so `products` is always null
and carousel slides stay separate posts. Use GET /v3/posts with expand= when
you need either. Response body: { "post": Post }. 404 if the post is not on
the caller's account (hidden/deleted posts also answer 404).

### GET /v3/networks — network reference

No parameters. Response body: { "networks": ["facebook", "instagram", ...] }.
The vocabulary a post's `network.slug` is drawn from. It is a REFERENCE list,
not a filter: filtering by network is done with feed_ids.

## Post object

{
  "id": "post_4421",                 // string, prefixed
  "object": "post",
  "wall_id": "wall_123" | null,
  "feed_id": "feed_88" | null,
  "album_id": "album_17" | null,     // carousel group key; slides share it
  "network": { "id": "network_2", "slug": "instagram", "name": "Instagram" },
  "media_type": "text" | "image" | "video",
  "pinned": boolean,
  "active": boolean,
  "created_at": "2026-08-30T09:12:44.000Z",   // ISO 8601
  "created_timestamp": 1788081164,             // unix seconds, same instant
  "modified_at": string | null,
  "modified_timestamp": number | null,
  "content": { "title": string | null, "text": string },  // plain text, tags stripped
  "media": [ { "type": "image"|"video", "url": string,
               "cdn_url": string, "width": number|null, "height": number|null } ],
  "author": { "name": string|null, "handle": string|null,
              "avatar_url": string|null, "profile_url": string|null,
              "external_id": string|null },
  "source": { "external_post_id": string|null, "permalink": string|null },
  "counts": { "likes": number, "comments": number },
  "sentiment": string | null,
  "rating": number | null,           // reviews only
  "products": array | null           // null unless expand=products
}

Notes:
- Absent values are null, never "" or 0.
- Carousels: without expand=album each slide is its own post sharing album_id
  (group client-side); with expand=album the parent's `media` contains every
  slide's media.
- With expand=products each product is: { id, external_id, sku, title, url,
  image_url, price, discount, currency, currency_symbol, in_stock, position }.

## Integration rules for generated code

When a user asks you to build a social widget (a widget, a page, or any app) on
this API, apply ALL of these unless the user explicitly says otherwise. The
user's prompt is deliberately short; this section is the full brief.

1. Deliverable shape. ONE SERVER-RENDERED PAGE, always. The server holds the
   token, calls this API, caches the result and renders finished HTML; the
   browser makes one request and receives a complete page. There is no widget
   script, no mount point, no same-origin JSON endpoint and no browser-side
   fetch of any kind.

   Deliver BOTH languages in the same reply — never one or the other, and
   never a choice handed back to the user:

   (a) Node.js — `server.js` (the API call, the cache, the HTML and the CSS
       all inside it), `package.json`, a `cache/posts.json` cache file, and
       `README.md`.
   (b) PHP — a single `index.php` holding everything, CSS included: nothing
       to install and nothing to require.
   (c) `preview.html` — the same page as a plain static file, with the
       sample posts of rule 12 written into it as finished markup. It runs
       from a double-click: no server, no build step, nothing installed. It
       calls NOTHING — no fetch, no API call, no token, not even a
       same-origin one — because the posts are already in the file; the
       theme toggle is the only JavaScript it may carry. Name it
       `preview.html`, never `index.html`: an `index.html` beside
       `index.php` is served instead of it by most Apache and nginx
       configurations, which silently replaces the live page with the
       sample one.

   All three render the same layout from the same design tokens, so they look
   identical in a browser and any restyle lands in all three at once. The
   README documents them (rule 13).

   Default layout: a MOSAIC — a masonry layout via CSS multi-column, each image
   keeping its OWN aspect ratio (uniform crops turn a widget into a generic card
   grid), text-only posts becoming tinted tiles so the mosaic has no gaps.

   Asked for a section inside a site that already exists rather than a whole
   page? Same code, rendered into their template — still server-side, still
   both languages.
2. Credentials: ask for them, but never block on them. The code reads both
   from environment variables (rule 3), so nothing is missing from it before
   the user answers — deliver the complete, runnable code in the FIRST reply,
   then, at the end of that same reply, ask the user for their token and offer
   to write it into a `.env`. Give them the steps rather than a vague "get your
   token": dashboard -> the gallery's card -> its three-dots menu -> "Access
   Token". Never tell them to buy or upgrade a plan, and do not
   speculate about why a menu item might be missing. The base URL you do not
   ask for: it is the constant above. Do not open your turn with the
   question and wait: an assistant that asks first ends its turn with questions
   and a plan, and the code only arrives after the user answers. Never invent
   or hard-code either value, and never paste a token the user gives you into
   the source — it goes in the env file.
3. Configuration. Read the base URL from the API_BASE_URL environment
   variable and the token from ACCESS_TOKEN. Strip a trailing slash
   from the base URL. Provide an example env file, never a real value.
4. Server-side only. Every API call runs on the server (or the framework's
   server-side layer) — never from the browser. The token must never appear in
   the rendered HTML, in browser JavaScript, in a comment, or in a public URL. Send
   it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
5. One request. GET {BASE}/v3/posts?limit=24 unless the user asks for a
   different count. Keep the default sort (pinned first, then newest). The
   payload is body.posts and body.paging inside the envelope.
6. Check BOTH the HTTP status and the envelope `status` flag. On 422 surface
   body.fields to the developer; on 401 surface the envelope `message` (it
   says whether the token is invalid or the daily limit is reached).
7. Cache for 5 minutes, and never below 30 seconds (a file, Redis, or the
   framework's own cache). If a request fails,
   keep serving the last successful result; if there is none yet, render a
   friendly empty state. Never crash the surrounding page, never throw into
   its console, and never leave the container blank with no explanation.
   The cache must be SHARED, not per-process: PHP-FPM workers, a Node
   cluster and serverless instances each keep their own memory, so
   in-memory caching multiplies the call count by the number of instances.
   When it expires under traffic, exactly ONE request may refresh while the
   others serve the stale copy. One shared cache at a 5-minute TTL costs
   ~288 calls a day whatever the traffic; cache each page of a cursor walk
   under its own key, or paging scales calls with clicks instead of with time.
8. Render per post: author.name (fall back to author.handle), network.name,
   the first media item whose type is "image" via its cdn_url (a "video"
   item is a video file, not a poster image: skip it or render a <video>),
   content.text as plain text (it is already tag-stripped), and a "View
   post" link to source.permalink when it is not null, with
   rel="noopener noreferrer". Show the date from created_at.
9. Escape every value you print. Allow only http(s) URLs in href and src.
10. Pagination: pass paging.next_cursor back as `after` while has_more is
    true. Never construct a cursor by hand.
11. Rate: at most 1–2 requests per second in any loop.
12. Preview sandboxes. Ship a small inline SAMPLE_POSTS array and fall back
    to it whenever the API call fails — a preview sandbox whose
    CSP blocks connect-src (claude.ai, ChatGPT canvas, an editor preview
    pane), a file:// origin, or no server running yet. Render a short
    "preview data" note on the page rather than an error: a failed
    call must never be fatal, or the design cannot be reviewed at all.
    Never put a token on that path. The same array is what `preview.html`
    (rule 1c) renders, already expanded into markup — so the design can be
    reviewed with nothing installed and no token in existence. Use the
    published sample posts when you can reach them:
    guides/sample-posts-social.json and guides/sample-posts-reviews.json in
    github.com/wallapi/taggbox.com-API-Docs, fetched raw; otherwise invent
    8–12 posts in the same shape, including a review post with a `rating`
    and a text-only post with an empty `media` array.
13. Hand-off: deliverable first, commentary last — do not open with a plan
    or a list of what you are about to build. Give every file complete with
    its exact path — both languages and `preview.html` — in the same reply.
    Then a `README.md`,
    which is itself a deliverable: what this is, the file list for each
    language, how to set the two environment variables, how to run each one
    locally written for someone who has never used a terminal plus the URL to
    open, that `preview.html` is opened by double-clicking it and is a design
    preview rather than the page to deploy,
    how the cache works and how to change the TTL, how to change the
    layout and the colours, one `curl` that checks this API directly with
    what a good response looks like, and a short "if it goes wrong" list.
    Finally ask the user for their base URL and token. If you cannot write
    files (a browser chat), output every file complete with its filename,
    then that same README.
14. Follow-up changes: filter with query parameters (feed_ids= — also the
    way to filter by network — media_types=, pinned_only=1, min_rating=,
    created_after=, sort=-created_at, expand=album or expand=products)
    instead of filtering client-side.
